messages.subject: Re: [TMB users] Changing Parameters amongst models on-the-fly
messages.subject_clean: [TMB users] Changing Parameters amongst models on-the-fly
messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob, you can use the "map" feature to selectively turn off parameter estimation while calling MakeADFun, then use a flag inside the template for your calculations. People often use this for similar reasons as what I understand you're asking for. I'm not aware of any examples with the map feature but I think it's documented on the R side.

It actually would be a good example to add to the list: full demonstration of the map capabilities.

-Cole

On Mon, Mar 5, 2018 at 8:57 PM, Robert OBoyle <betas...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi TMB users
>
> I have two models, the difference between which is the list of parameters used (there are other differences but not germane to my question). I am exploring if I can change the PARAMETER declarations in the cpp file dependent on an input model flag. For example,
>
> ...
>
> DATA_INTEGER(model_no);   where model_no is input as an integer such as 1, 2, etc
> ...
>
> I tried using the switch command (with the appropriate parms set up in the r file) as:
>
>   switch(model_no)
>   {
>    case 1:
>     PARAMETER_MATRIX(parm1_mat);
>     PARAMETER_VECTOR(parm1_vect);
>    break;
>
>    case 2:
>     PARAMETER_VECTOR(parm2_vect);
>     PARAMETER(parm2);
>    break;
>   }
>
> but this doesn't seem to work. Can switch or other c++ syntax be used to change TMB parameters on-the-fly? Am I missing something?
>
> Any insight is much appreciated.
>
> Bob

messages.subject_clean: [TMB users] Changing Parameters amongst models on-the-fly
messages.body_plain:
In addition to the map feature here are a few more options:

1. Control the case you're in from R by passing zero-length objects:

PARAMETER_MATRIX(parm1_mat);
PARAMETER_VECTOR(parm1_vect);
PARAMETER_VECTOR(parm2_vect);
PARAMETER(parm2);

int model_no;
if (parm1_mat.size() > 0) model_no = 1;
if (parm2_vect.size() > 0) model_no = 2;

2. Conditionally pass parameter objects (but not until you need them):

DATA_INTEGER(model_no);

if (model_no == 1) {
  PARAMETER_MATRIX(parm1_mat);   // Local to the branch
  PARAMETER_VECTOR(parm1_vect);  // Local to the branch
  // Here comes procedure depending on parameters
}

messages.body_plain:
Hi Kasper

I tried the if syntax to select between models and found out a few things.

If a PARAMETER declaration is within an if loop, then pretty much all references to the declared parameter have to be within that loop. I tried using a parameter outside the loop and I got 'not declared in scope' errors. This was also the case for a REPORT statement.

I also tried the switch command rather than the if syntax and couldn't get it to work. Not sure why as I have other code (e.g. SAM) in which it does. I'll use the if syntax unless you or anyone else can identify some special issues with the switch command that I should be aware of.

Thanks again

Bob

messages.subject_clean: [TMB users] Changing Parameters amongst models on-the-fly
messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,

This is all as expected: Calculations referring to a parameter declared inside a block must be within that same block. The same holds for REPORT statements.

However, note the following trick to get a parameter from 'local scope' to 'global scope':

Type a_;
if (true) {
  PARAMETER(a);
  a_ = a;
}

The switch statement cannot be used as variable declarations inside 'switch' are not allowed.

Cheers,
Kasper

messages.subject: Data augmentation with TMB?
messages.body_plain:
Dear TMB users,

I am currently fitting state space models using TMB and I would like to know if anyone have already implemented data augmentation in this package.

My data consist of time series of 3 simultaneous types of observations of latent processes (dynamics of experimental populations of microalgae replicated in batch). I would like to fit a state space model on this data set, but many observations are missing:

-  For two observation methods, I cannot get population size estimation when the number of individuals is too low

-  For the last observation method, I got data only half of the time.

I became aware that points in the latent process would not affect equally the likelihood when they do not have the same number of observations, which may be a problem to estimate process parameters.

I would appreciate any suggestions to deal with this problem.

Thanks,

Marie

I am thinking of submitting an abstract along the following lines:

> In a recent and popular stats.stackexchange post, the following question was asked:
>
>
>
> “I bet with my colleague that I will beat him in fifty consecutive ping pong games. So far I have won 15, what are my chances of winning the next 35 games?”
>
>
>
> -- from https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/329521/
>
>
>
> To answer this question, I model the OP (original poster) as a far superior player who still wishes to make the game fun for their opponent (they are colleagues after all). This leads to a regression problem for the OP’s probability of winning a point, that cannot be fit using standard regression packages. This talk will demonstrate how to use the Template Model Builder (TMB) package with an optimisation algorithm to find maximum likelihood estimates for the regression coefficients. It will also briefly touch upon the role of automatic differentiation in optimisation and C++ integration with R.

So no constrained optimisation and the dataset is small. But, with some thought in the next few months I might be able to simulate a dataset under a reasonable data generation process so that I can fit a constrained optimisation. Do you have any thoughts? Would you find such a talk interesting enough to attend?

messages.subject_clean: [TMB users] Handling list of numerous vectors with DATA_STRUCT ?
messages.body_plain:
How about representing the multiple time series as a vector and a factor ?
Example:

In R we can do

x <- 1:10
f <- gl(2,5)
spl <- split(x,f)

In TMB:

PARAMETER_VECTOR(x);
DATA_FACTOR(f);
vector<vector<Type> > spl = split(x, f);

You can loop through the split like this:

for (int i=0; i<NLEVELS(f); i++) {
  vector<Type> xi = spl(i);
}

messages.subject: too many questions about Lambert W function in TMB
messages.subject_clean: too many questions about Lambert W function in TMB
messages.body_plain:
I have an application (functional responses in a predator-prey
system with depletion) for which the predicted value involves the
result of a Lambert W function
<https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambert_W_function>. (I only need this
for positive real inputs, so there's no messing around with
complex-valued or multi-valued functions.)

  It's not too hard to write C++ code to compute W(z) (in fact there's
already some code in the TMB codebase for this, in the one-step-ahead
residual computation), but all of the ways I know to compute this are
iterative, which means that they will involve if() statements, even
though the final output is continuous (at least as far as it can be in
floating-point).

  I *think* this means that I need to define a new "primitive" (the
term in adcomp seems to be "atomic"?) function to tell TMB that W(z)
has a specified derivative W'(z) [maybe I also need to define W''(z)]
?  So far I haven't been able to find any examples/documentation of
how I would do this ...

  By analogy with ADMB (chapter 13 of the the manual), I need to write
new adjoint code.  The TODO file for the adcomp package
https://github.com/kaskr/adcomp/blob/master/TODO.md includes 'Make

wow! thanks!  there's so much in here that, while reasonably easy to
understand once you've done it for me, would have taken days to figure
out for myself. Let me know if you want assistance in writing up the
explanation of this in a way that will be comprehensible to a newbie
like myself ...

FWIW more efficient iterative special-purpose algorithms to compute
Lambert-W exist, but I think Newton's method will work just fine.  (If
I get  ambitious maybe I'll try to use your example as a template to
code one of them up: I don't think I'd have to do anything but replace
the body of the plain-C++ code ...)

  cheers
    Ben Bolker

On Wed, Mar 28, 2018 at 10:57 AM, Kasper Kristensen
<kasper.k...@gmail.com> wrote:
> You're right Ben. This can be handled with 'atomic functions'. The Lambert W
> function is a great example which should be put in the manual. Here's a
> first pass:
>
> #include <TMB.hpp>
>
> // Step 1: Code up a plain C version
> double W(double x) {
>   double reltol = 1.490116e-08;
>   double logx = log(x);
>   double y = (logx > 0 ? logx : 0);
>   int niter = 100;
>   int i=0;
>   for (; i < niter; i++) {
>     if ( fabs( logx - log(y) - y) < reltol) break;
>     double fdivg = (y - exp(logx - y)) / (1 + y);
>     y = y - fdivg;
>   }
>   if (i == niter) Rf_warning("W: failed convergence");
>   return y;
> }
>
> // Step 2: Code up reverse mode derivatives:
> // x = W(x) * exp( W(x) )
> // W'(x) = 1 / ( exp(W(x)) * (1 + W(x)) )
> TMB_ATOMIC_VECTOR_FUNCTION(
>                // ATOMIC_NAME
>                W
>                ,
>                // OUTPUT_DIM
>                1,
>                // ATOMIC_DOUBLE
>                double x = tx[0]; // input
>                            ty[0] = W(x);     // output
>                ,
>                // ATOMIC_REVERSE
>                Type W = ty[0];   // Function value
>                px[0] = 1. / (exp(W) * (1. + W)) * py[0];
>                )
>
> // Step 3: Make version with scalar arguments:
> template<class Type>
> Type W(Type x){
>   CppAD::vector<Type> tx(1);
>   tx[0] = x;
>   return W(tx)[0];
> }
>
> template<class Type>
> Type objective_function<Type>::operator() ()
> {
>   PARAMETER(x);
>   Type f = W(x);
>   return f;
> }
>
>
